A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SSL4RL, with matching authors, framework, and substantial shared experimental content. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on MMBench, SEED-Bench, ImageNet, and graph benchmarks, alongside task-difficulty, model-size, and reward-combination experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds captioning, further visual benchmarks, supervised-RL comparisons, robustness tests, and additional ablations.

M1.justification: Appendix J adds two exploratory SSL tasks: identifying a masked patch and selecting a positive view among DINOv2-mined hard negatives. These extend the available reward tasks while retaining the original four visual tasks, graph tasks, and GRPO framework.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluations on V*, RealWorldQA, BLINK, MME-RealWorld-Lite, and CapArena image captioning, plus corrupted-image MMBench scenarios. These substantially broaden visual conditions and task requirements beyond the retained visual and graph benchmarks.

E2.justification: Appendix G introduces a VLM-R1-style Golden-3B baseline trained with downstream answer rewards and compared against SSL4RL on MMBench and SEED-Bench. CapArena additionally uses GPT-4o, CogVLM-19B, and MiniCPM-8B captions as comparators. v1 primarily compared SSL4RL variants with their base models.

E3.justification: Added studies introduce a 60/40 training/test split for the Golden-3B comparison, Gemma3-4B training with batch size 256, approximately 4,000/18,000/118,000-sample training regimes, and weak/strong corruption protocols. Captioning introduces GPT-4o judging, pairwise scores, and min-max normalization. These are additional protocols; the original Qwen GRPO settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained difficulty, model-size, combination, attention, and reward-curve analyses, v2 adds data-volume scaling, base-model choice, corruption robustness, harder-task experiments, and captioning case studies. It also extends documented difficulty analyses to ImageNet and adds entropy and response-length training diagnostics.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed studies, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The new entropy plots describe model behavior during training rather than uncertainty in experimental estimates.

E6.justification: Corresponding MMBench tables revise Jigsaw averages from 79.11 to 77.82 for 3B and from 86.27 to 87.73 for 7B. The 3B 3x3 Jigsaw result changes from 80.38 to 75.12, reversing its tabulated difficulty trend. Numerous new evaluation and ablation results are added, although Figures 4 and 5 retain outdated Jigsaw values.

T1.justification: Section 3 retains the corruption-based formulation, reward definitions, and regularized GRPO objective in Equation 1. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and the added task descriptions and empirical interpretations introduce no substantive mathematical development.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add claims about open-ended captioning benefits, and the abstract expands the identified design factors to include data volume and model choice. The central claims about verifiable SSL rewards, reasoning improvements, and cross-domain applicability remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of data scaling, architectural generality, corruption resilience, and proximity to oracle-reward performance. Appendix J supplements the diminishing-returns discussion with harder-task evidence, while Appendix K attributes entropy and response-length behavior to KL regularization and perception-focused tasks. The earlier task-alignment and negative-transfer qualifications remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds code and model-hosting identifiers, DINOv2-based negative construction details, and parameters for new evaluations. Original GRPO and hardware disclosures remain largely unchanged. The abstract announces released resources, but the reproducibility statement still promises code release upon acceptance, leaving release status internally inconsistent.

R1.justification: Section 2 newly credits Jigsaw-R1 as a direct predecessor and positions SSL4RL as generalizing that approach across tasks and domains. Appendix J also acknowledges concurrent Spatial-SSRL. This materially refines novelty positioning beyond v1's discussion of general SSL and self-reward literature, alongside additional method and benchmark citations.

P1.justification: Much of the introduction, framework, conclusion, and retained appendix prose remains unchanged. v2 reorders ImageNet evaluation and ablations, moves benchmark and graph details into appendices, and revises headings and transitions around the expanded experiments. This is localized restructuring rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial table and figure displays for captioning, oracle comparisons, robustness, scaling, Gemma, harder tasks, and training diagnostics. It splits the graph-results table and relocates SEED-Bench results. Figure 3 is reduced to one attention example; the other example remains available in the appendix.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for generality: the Golden-3B comparison addresses v1's lack of a trained RL comparator, while Gemma, corruption, and harder-task studies test previously unexamined boundaries. Explicitly acknowledging Jigsaw-R1 also improves novelty attribution. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, particularly stale Jigsaw plots and insufficiently explained CapArena score aggregation, although those issues still limit confidence in parts of the expanded evidence.
